name: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP)
lead: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a yellow crystalline industrial chemical that has been used in explosives, pesticides and dyes, and that was briefly sold as a weight-loss drug in the United States in the 1930s [1]. It acts as a mitochondrial uncoupler: it makes cells release energy as heat rather than storing it as ATP, which raises metabolic rate [1].

In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums, DNP is discussed as a very fast fat-loss compound, and users on looksmax.org describe cutting cycles lasting from a couple of weeks to a few weeks, often alongside other compounds [2][3][4]. It is not approved as a medicine anywhere that the sources describe; it is sold online as a research or industrial chemical [1].

Toxicology literature and regulators describe a very narrow gap between the doses that raise metabolism and doses that cause dangerous overheating (hyperthermia), and there is no specific antidote [1]. Published clinical weight-loss trials meeting modern standards were not found; the evidence is historical case experience, toxicology reports and forum anecdote.
infobox: Dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient as heat [1]
Not approved for human use; UK regulated poison since 2023; WADA-banned since 2015 [1]

paras: DNP is a protonophore: it carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane and so collapses the gradient that cells normally use to make ATP. The energy is lost as heat, and the body compensates by raising its metabolic rate, which is the basis of its fat-loss effect [1]. A general reference describes energy expenditure rising by roughly 30 to 40 percent [1].
A physiologically based pharmacokinetic model for DNP has been published in the research literature, reflecting continued academic interest in the compound's behaviour in the body [5].

DNP was linked to illness and some deaths among munitions workers in France during World War I [1]. In 1933 the Stanford researcher Maurice Tainter published results in which obese patients treated with DNP lost an average of about 20 pounds, and he later estimated that at least 100,000 people in the United States had been treated in the first year, with three reported deaths [1].

In 1935 the American Medical Association's Council on Chemistry and Pharmacy declined to list DNP, judging its risks to outweigh benefits, and cataract reports emerged that year [1]. The 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act expanded FDA authority, and DNP was deemed too toxic for human consumption [1]. In 1948 Loomis and Lipmann described its mechanism of action [1]. Its use outside medicine increased in the 21st century after it became widely available online [1].

The best-documented efficacy data are historical: the 1930s clinical reports of weight loss in obese patients [1]. No modern randomised controlled trial of DNP for fat loss was identified. Forum users report rapid weight loss; for example, one looksmax.org poster reported losing about 19.6 lb in 15 days while eating little, and another reported losing 8 to 10 lb of fat over 21 days alongside a calorie deficit and other compounds [2][6]. These are self-reports without controls.

DNP is described as having a low therapeutic index, meaning toxic doses are not far above those that produce effects [1]. Reported effects include rash, neuropathy, agranulocytosis, cataracts (sometimes with permanent vision loss), and rarely deafness [1]. Overdose is described as causing nausea, sweating, tachycardia, rapid breathing and uncontrolled hyperthermia, with body temperatures reaching 44 degrees C in fatal cases [1].

Symptoms can begin within about three hours of ingestion, and in published fatal cases the average time to death was around 14 hours [1]. A summary of poison-centre data for 2010 to 2020 reported an 11.9 percent fatality rate and at least 50 deaths worldwide in that period [1]. A 2006 toxicology report described two deaths attributed to DNP use, which T Nation members have cited in discussions [7]. Animal studies have found teratogenic, mutagenic and carcinogenic effects [1].

Users on looksmax.org describe the heat and fever in the early days of a cycle, lethargy, and sickness during use. One poster reported unbearable heat and fever by day 6 at about 400 mg per day and skipped doses [2].

In the United States DNP is classified as an explosive and has been designated an orphan drug for Huntington's disease; physician Nicholas Bachynsky was convicted of drug offences in 1986 and of fraud in 2008 after supplying DNP to patients [1]. In the United Kingdom a seller was convicted of manslaughter in 2018, and in 2020 of gross negligence manslaughter after a retrial; DNP became a regulated poison in October 2023 [1]. The World Anti-Doping Agency has banned it since 2015, and Interpol and WADA issued a warning that year [1].

DNP appears on looksmax.org in cutting logs, source-request threads and stack discussions with other fat-loss compounds such as clenbuterol, retatrutide and tirzepatide [2][6][8]. Posters often compare it with GLP-1-type compounds and cite specific cutting diets. Reactions in threads range from enthusiastic to alarmed; one reply to a log said the compound was known to be fatal, while the poster said it was manageable if hydration was maintained [2]. Another poster argued that a testosterone plus retatrutide plan with a structured diet would outperform DNP [3]. On T Nation, DNP has been discussed since at least 2007, with threads citing patents, a review of its acute toxicity and the 2006 fatality report [7][9].

No studies found for DNP as a modern fat-loss treatment. Historical 1930s clinical reports are summarised above [1]. Related laboratory research has examined DNP in cell models of neurodegeneration, in which a 2024 study reported protective effects against okadaic acid toxicity in cultured cells [10]. Many other literature hits for the abbreviation DNP concern unrelated subjects such as nuclear polarisation, nurse practitioner degrees and anti-DNP antibody assays.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org DNP is discussed as a rapid fat-loss compound used for cutting before events or at the start of a season, usually stacked with other compounds, and members trade experience logs and source requests [2][3][6].

claims.claim: DNP is a "super effective cut" that produces about 8-10 lb of fat loss in three weeks.
claims.believers: Users report large short-term weight drops, such as roughly 19.6 lb in 15 days, with little or no training, attributing it to the compound [2][6].
claims.experts: Mechanistic literature agrees that uncoupling raises energy expenditure, but no modern controlled trial has quantified fat loss, and self-reported scale weight can include water [1].

claims.claim: The risks are manageable with hydration, avoiding summer heat and starting at lower doses.
claims.believers: Posters say they survived multi-week cycles and that side effects such as heat and fever faded after adjusting, and that fear of death is exaggerated [2][6].
claims.experts: Toxicology sources describe a narrow therapeutic index, no antidote, fatal hyperthermia, and an 11.9 percent fatality rate in poison-centre reports from 2010 to 2020 [1].

claims.claim: Testosterone plus retatrutide and a structured diet outperforms DNP, so DNP is unnecessary.
claims.believers: Some members argue modern peptides, low-dose testosterone and aggressive calorie control give comparable results with fewer dangers [3].
claims.experts: No published head-to-head comparison between DNP and these combinations was found.

claims.claim: DNP can be sourced online from supplement vendors or EU suppliers.
claims.believers: Members regularly ask for and share sources, including in Europe [6][11].
claims.experts: In the UK it is a regulated poison since 2023, a seller has been convicted of manslaughter, and WADA bans it [1].

card.summary: A 1930s diet drug that melts fat by turning cells into heaters; the narrow gap between effective and lethal is why it is banned for human use.
card.note: Fatal overheating with no antidote; regulated poison in the UK since 2023; banned by WADA.

quick.overview:
DNP is an industrial chemical that was sold as a diet pill in the 1930s before being judged too toxic. It reappeared in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles as a very fast fat burner, with users reporting several pounds lost per week.

Evidence for its fat-loss effect is historical and anecdotal; no modern controlled trials exist. The mechanism is well understood, but the safety margin is described as very narrow.
quick.mechanism: DNP shuttles protons across the mitochondrial membrane, so cells burn fuel and release the energy as heat instead of making ATP. Metabolic rate rises, and so does body temperature.
quick.risks: Reported harms include overheating (hyperthermia) up to fatal temperatures, cataracts, rash, and blood and organ damage. There is no antidote. It is not approved for human use; the UK made it a regulated poison in 2023, a seller has been convicted of manslaughter, and WADA bans it.
